title: Greedy and backtracking: concepts and counts
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, bits and CIDR, DP, greedy, backtracking and mock-interview habits, in pseudocode. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: When greedy works and how to prove it, activity selection, jump game, gas station, then subsets, permutations, combination sum, N-Queens and pruning (no language-specific code).
source: CLRS ch. 16; MIT 6.046 greedy notes; LeetCode Jump Game, Gas Station, Subsets I/II, Permutations II, Combination Sum; NeetCode backtracking roadmap

questions.prompt: Activities as (start, finish): (1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11), (8,12), (2,14), (12,16). An activity may start exactly when another finishes. What is the maximum number of activities one person can attend?
questions.explanation: Sort by finish and pick greedily: (1,4), (5,7), (8,11), (12,16) = 4. No schedule of 5 exists; the earliest-finish rule is optimal.

questions.prompt: Gas station circuit: gas = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and cost = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]. Station i gives gas[i] and the trip to the next station costs cost[i]. At which index (0-based) must you start to complete the circle?
questions.explanation: Total gas 15 equals total cost 15, so a solution exists. Reset the start whenever the running tank goes negative: it fails at 0, 1, 2 and the start becomes 3. From 3 the tank runs 3, 6, 4, 2, 0 and never goes negative.

questions.prompt: How many distinct permutations does the multiset {A, A, B, C} have?
questions.explanation: 4! / 2! = 24 / 2 = 12. A backtracking solution that sorts the input and skips equal neighbours (using a used[] array) produces exactly 12 leaves; a naive one produces 24 with duplicates.

questions.prompt: Candidates [2, 3, 6, 7] (each may be reused any number of times) and target 7. How many distinct combinations sum to 7?
questions.explanation: [2,2,3] and [7] are the only two. Every other path either overshoots 7 or leaves a remainder of 1, which no candidate can fill. Sorting and breaking when a candidate exceeds the remainder prunes the search.

questions.prompt: How many distinct ways can 6 queens be placed on a 6 x 6 board so that none attacks another?
questions.explanation: The counts for n = 1..8 are 1, 0, 0, 2, 10, 4, 40, 92. Backtracking places one queen per row and prunes with sets for used columns and both diagonals (r - c and r + c), far less work than the n^n raw placements.

questions.prompt: For nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], where nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i, what is the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index?
questions.explanation: 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 is 3 jumps. The O(n) greedy keeps the end of the current jump range and the farthest index reachable; each time you pass the range end you count one more jump.

questions.prompt: What does an exchange argument show about a greedy algorithm?
questions.explanation: For activity selection: take any optimal schedule, swap its first activity for the earliest-finishing one; it still fits and has the same size.

options.text: Any optimal solution can be reshaped into the greedy one without getting worse.
options.why: Correct: swapping step by step to the greedy choice never loses value, so greedy is optimal.

options.text: The greedy choice is optimal on every random test you ran, including large ones.
options.why: Testing builds confidence but is not a proof; an exchange argument is a proof.

options.text: The algorithm runs in O(n log n) because it sorts the input first and then scans once.
options.why: That is a running-time statement, unrelated to correctness.

options.text: Every subproblem is solved once and cached in a table for later reuse.
options.why: That describes dynamic programming, not an exchange argument.

questions.prompt: Maximising the number of non-overlapping meetings in a room.
questions.explanation: Earliest start fails on one long meeting that starts first and blocks many short ones.
questions.assertion: Sort by earliest finish time, not earliest start time.
questions.reason: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the remaining meetings, which an exchange argument proves.

whys.a: Right: R is the justification that A is the correct rule.
whys.b: R is the justification, not an unrelated fact.

questions.prompt: Making change with the fewest coins.
questions.explanation: Whether greedy works depends on the coin system. For arbitrary coins use DP.
questions.assertion: Taking the largest coin that fits at each step gives the fewest coins for any coin system.
questions.reason: Largest-first is optimal for the coin system {1, 5, 10, 25}.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: A is false because of counterexamples like {1,5,6,9} with 11 (greedy 3 coins, optimal 2); R is true for canonical systems such as US coins.

questions.prompt: In Combination Sum with reusable candidates.
questions.explanation: The index controls which candidates remain available; the remaining value controls termination. Mixing these up is a common bug.
questions.assertion: Recursing with the same index i, not i + 1, lets a candidate be used again.
questions.reason: Each recursive call subtracts the chosen candidate from the remaining target.

whys.a: R does not explain why reuse is allowed.
whys.b: Right: both are true; reuse comes from the index, while subtracting the candidate is how the target shrinks.

questions.prompt: Jump Game: can you reach the last index when nums[i] is the maximum jump from i?
questions.explanation: Backtracking or memoised DP also work but cost far more; the greedy keeps a single number, the farthest reachable index.
questions.assertion: The farthest-reach greedy solves Jump Game in O(n) time.
questions.reason: It explores every possible jump sequence with backtracking.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true because the reachable indices form a prefix, but the greedy does not enumerate sequences, so R is false.

questions.prompt: True or false: to maximise the number of non-overlapping activities, always pick the shortest remaining activity first.
questions.explanation: Only earliest-finish-time is provably optimal; earliest-start and shortest-first both have counterexamples.

options.why: A short activity placed in the middle of two long ones can block both, so shortest-first fails.
Correct: shortest-first has counterexamples; earliest finish is the proven rule.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: for which problems does a simple greedy rule give a provably optimal answer?
questions.explanation: Greedy needs the greedy-choice property. When you cannot prove it, test with small counterexamples and fall back to DP.

options.text: Activity selection by earliest finish time.
options.why: Correct: the exchange argument proves it.

options.text: 0/1 knapsack by value per unit weight.
options.why: A high ratio item can waste capacity; counterexamples exist, so use DP.

options.text: Fractional knapsack by value per unit weight.
options.why: Correct: filling the best ratios first is optimal when items can be split.

options.text: Coin change for the arbitrary coin set {1, 5, 6, 9}.
options.why: Largest-first gives 3 coins for 11 where 2 is possible.

questions.prompt: Complete the rule for subsets of an array that may contain duplicates.
questions.explanation: Sorting groups equal values. Skipping a repeat only at the same recursion level (i > start) still allows [2,2] while removing a duplicate [2] branch. [1,2,2] yields 6 unique subsets instead of 8.
questions.text: First {1} the array. In the loop, skip nums[i] when i > start and nums[i] == nums[{2}]. A set of n distinct items has {3} subsets.

questions.prompt: Match each enumeration with the number of results (leaves) it produces.
questions.explanation: Subsets: include/exclude per item. Permutations: n choices, then n-1, ... Combinations: n-choose-k. Parentheses: Catalan numbers (1, 2, 5, 14 for n = 1..4). Total work multiplies by the cost of copying each result.

left.text: All subsets of n distinct items
All permutations of n distinct items
All combinations of k items chosen from n
All valid strings of n pairs of parentheses

questions.prompt: When generating all valid strings of n pairs of parentheses by backtracking, which rule prunes the search so only valid strings are built?
questions.explanation: The result count is the Catalan number: 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 for n = 1..5. The pattern 'add only while the prefix stays valid' is the general way to prune backtracking.

options.text: Add ")" first whenever possible, and "(" only when no ")" fits.
options.why: Closing first produces invalid prefixes such as ")(" immediately.

options.text: Add "(" while fewer than n are used, and ")" only while closes < opens.
options.why: Correct: the prefix stays valid at every step, so no dead branches are explored.

options.text: Build every string of length 2n and test each one for balance at the end.
options.why: That enumerates 2^(2n) strings instead of pruning during construction.

options.text: Allow "(" and ")" equally, then drop results with unequal counts.
options.why: Equal counts are not enough: ")(" has equal counts but is invalid.

questions.prompt: Write pseudocode for the greedy that returns the maximum number of non-overlapping activities from a list of (start, finish) pairs, where an activity may start exactly when the previous one finishes.
questions.explanation: Sorting dominates, so the total is O(n log n). The >= test lets an activity start exactly when the previous one ends. The earliest-finish rule is justified by an exchange argument.

checks.label: sorts the activities by finish time
keeps the finish time of the last chosen activity
takes an activity when its start is at or after that finish

questions.model:
sort activities by finish time
last_end = -infinity; count = 0
for (s, f) in sorted activities:
    if s >= last_end:
        count = count + 1
        last_end = f
return count
